verses.text: In the days of Amraphel, king of Shinar, Arioch, king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Tidal, king of Goiim,
they made war with Bera, king of Sodom, and with Birsha, king of Gomorrah, Shinab, king of Admah, and Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (also called Zoar).
All these joined together in the valley of Siddim (also called the Salt Sea).
They served Chedorlaomer for twelve years, and in the thirteenth year, they rebelled.
In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, and the kings who were with him, and struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzim in Ham, and the Emim in Shaveh Kiriathaim,
and the Horites in their Mount Seir, to El Paran, which is by the wilderness.
They returned, and came to En Mishpat (also called Kadesh), and struck all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites, that lived in Hazazon Tamar.

The king of Sodom, and the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Admah, and the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (also called Zoar) went out; and they set the battle in array against them in the valley of Siddim;
against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings against the five.
Now the valley of Siddim was full of tar pits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and some fell there, and those who remained fled to the hills.
They took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their food, and went their way.
They took Lot, Abram’s brother’s son, who lived in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.
One who had escaped came and told Abram, the Hebrew. At that time, he lived by the oaks of Mamre, the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner; and they were allies of Abram.
When Abram heard that his relative was taken captive, he led out his trained men, born in his house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued as far as Dan.
He divided himself against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them, and pursued them to Hobah, which is on the left hand of Damascus.
He brought back all the goods, and also brought back his relative, Lot, and his goods, and the women also, and the other people.
The king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, at the valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley).
Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High.
He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth:
and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Abram gave him a tenth of all.
The king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people, and take the goods for yourself.”
Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth,
that I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap nor anything that is yours, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’
I will accept nothing from you except that which the young men have eaten, and the portion of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them take their portion.”

footnotes.content: I notice how the Lord carefully records names of kings long forgotten. Before Abram ever lifts a sword, the stage is already set by earthly powers, yet the God who calls Abram will prove Himself far greater than all of them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: War brews between city-kings of the plain and a coalition from the east. I learn early that rebellion against authority can lead to bitter conflict, and the cities of the plain will soon learn the weight of their own choices.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They gather in the Valley of Siddim, which is also the Salt Sea. How fitting that a place of bitter waters becomes the stage for both human pride and, soon, divine rescue. The geography itself whispers of judgment to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve years of servitude, and in the thirteenth they rebel. I see how patience runs thin and pride rises when people grow weary of yoke-bearing. Yet the God who ordains kings will also use their rebellion to draw Abram onto the scene for Lot's sake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chedorlaomer's campaign sweeps through ancient tribes with fearsome names. I take note that God's promises to Abram are not safe from conflict in this world, but the One who gave those promises still watches over the heir of the promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They press to the edge of the wilderness, driving before them. I see how the strong prey on the vulnerable in a fallen world. But Abram, soon to be called forth, will prove a very different sort of man—one who fights not for plunder, but for kin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They return through En-Mishpat, striking down those in their path. I am sobered by the trail of conquest. Yet our God is not blind to such days; He will raise up a champion from among His own to turn the tide for the sake of love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The five kings of the plain muster for battle in Siddim. I see how quickly alliances form when facing a common threat. But without the Lord, even a coalition of cities proves no match for the judgment that was already approaching them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four kings against five—a lopsided match turned on its head. I am reminded that numbers are never decisive with the Lord. The real question will not be who has the larger army, but who trusts the God of heaven and earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The valley is full of tar pits, and kings flee to fall therein. How tragic that the very ground meant to hold them becomes their snare. I see a picture of sinners fleeing from judgment, only to find the world they trusted offers no sure refuge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The victors plunder Sodom and Gomorrah of all they possess. I see how quickly the goods of the wicked become spoil for others. Earthly treasures, held apart from the Lord, prove to be no security when the day of upheaval comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They take Lot, Abram's brother's son, who dwelt in Sodom. I am grieved that Lot, for all his association with Abram, had chosen to pitch his tent toward Sodom. Yet grace will reach him through his uncle's faithful love, pointing us to a greater Kinsman who rescues His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fugitive brings word to Abram the Hebrew, dwelling by the oaks of Mamre. I love that Abram is called 'the Hebrew' here—set apart from the surrounding nations. Surrounded by Amorite allies, he yet looks to a different help, and now love compels him to action for Lot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hearing of Lot's capture, Abram arms his trained men, three hundred and eighteen born in his house, and pursues to Dan. I see faith moving into faithful action. This is no reckless raid, but the love of a kinsman-redeemer rising up, a faint shadow of Jesus who leaves all to rescue His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By night Abram divides his men and strikes the enemy, pursuing to Hobah near Damascus. I take courage that the Lord grants wisdom and victory to one man trusting Him against a great host. Our God still delights to use faithful obedience, however small the numbers, for the good of His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram brings back all the goods, Lot and his goods, the women and the people. I rejoice in this gentle triumph of grace-filled love. He recovers what was lost without grasping it for himself, showing us the heart of our true Redeemer who restores all that sin has stolen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Sodom comes out to meet Abram in the Valley of Shaveh, the King's Valley. Two kings meet after the battle—one representing a doomed city, the other a pilgrim who trusts the God Most High. Already I sense the contrast between what the world offers and what faithfulness receives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine. Here breaks in a mysterious figure, greater in type than Abram himself, pointing to the One who is both King and Priest forever. My heart longs for Jesus, our true Melchizedek, who brings us His own body and blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Melchizedek blesses Abram in the name of God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth. I bow with Abram, for all blessing flows from that God alone. How precious that before any reward from Sodom, Abram receives blessing from the Priest of the true God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blessed be God Most High, who delivered Abram's enemies into his hand. Abram gives Melchizedek a tenth of all, acknowledging that the victory belongs to the Lord. In doing so, he tithes to a greater priest, humbly confessing that every good gift comes from above.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Sodom offers Abram the people and the goods for himself. I see the world's way—after using others, it would reward the rescuer with spoil. But Abram has already been blessed by God Most High, and he will not let the king of Sodom steal the glory that belongs to his God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram lifts his hand to Yahweh, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth, and swears he will take nothing. What a testimony! He would rather be poor and owe nothing to Sodom, than rich and give Sodom reason to boast. Faith trusts the Possessor of all to provide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He will not take so much as a thread or sandal strap, lest Sodom say, 'I have made Abram rich.' I am convicted by his zeal for God's glory. May I, too, refuse to let the world take credit for what my God has freely given by grace through faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in Abram's restraint: the greatest wealth is to owe all to God Most High. As of 2026-10, I look back with gratitude that our true Abram, Jesus, refused all the kingdoms of this world to rescue us, giving us instead the riches of His own kingdom forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
